title: OI Spurts Explained: How to Read NSE's OI Spurts Data
summary: Understand OI spurts with examples. Learn how to read NSE open interest changes alongside price and volume, and distinguish long buildup from short covering.
body_markdown:
## What Are OI Spurts?


OI spurts are sudden, substantial increases in[open interest](https://algotest.in/blog/oi-in-options-trading) —the number of outstanding futures or options contracts over a selected period. They indicate that outstanding positions have increased, but do not establish a bullish or bearish direction. Traders interpret OI changes alongside price, volume and the contract’s expiry.


OI-change screeners may also show sharp decreases, which indicate a net reduction in outstanding positions. Check whether the figures compare the current reading with the previous trading day or another selected interval.

## How Do You Interpret OI Spurts with Price?


For a futures contract, traders commonly use the following framework. Compare price and OI over the same period.


Futures price


Open interest


Common interpretation


Rises


Rises


Long buildup


Falls


Rises


Short buildup


Rises


Falls


Short covering


Falls


Falls


Long unwinding


These labels describe price-and-OI patterns; they do not prove traders’ motives or predict the next price move.


For options, also check whether the contract is a call or put, its strike, expiry and implied volatility. An increase in call OI alone does not establish call writing or a bearish outlook.


## Where Can You Check NSE OI Spurts?


Visit NSE’s[Change in Open Interest page](https://www.nseindia.com/market-data/oi-spurts) , which retains “oi-spurts” in its URL. Check the displayed timestamp before interpreting the figures.


When assessing an OI spurt, compare the percentage change with the starting OI, absolute change, trading volume and liquidity. A large percentage increase from a small base can exaggerate the apparent significance of the activity.


### The calculation


OI change % = (Current OI − Previous OI) ÷ Previous OI × 100


If a contract held 1,00,000 contracts yesterday and holds 1,30,000 today, that is a 30% increase. The arithmetic is the easy part. What the figure means depends on the price move, the traded volume and how close you are to expiry, all covered below.

### The Two Levels of Detail


The page offers two views, and knowing which one you are looking at changes what the numbers mean.


-


**By Underlying** combines the OI change across all contracts of a symbol. It tells you positioning in a stock or index has shifted, but not where.


-


**By Contracts** shows each contract, with instrument type, expiry, strike, option type and last traded price. This is where you find which strike the activity is in.


The contract view also groups contracts by how OI and price moved together, which matches the four patterns in the table above. For more practice with these patterns on the index, see our guide on[how to read Nifty OI data](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-read-nifty-oi-data/) .


To see one underlying across every strike at once, the option chain is the better tool. We cover it in our guide on[how to read the Nifty option chain](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-read-nifty-option-chain-step-by-step-for-traders/) .


## Reading the Numbers


### Why % change matters more than absolute change


A liquid name like Reliance can add a large absolute number of contracts and barely register as a percentage, because its base open interest is already huge. A mid-cap F&O stock can add a much smaller absolute number and show a 40% jump.


The percentage figure is what surfaces the second case, and the second case is usually the more interesting one. A 40% move means the positioning profile of that contract has genuinely changed today.


Absolute change still has a use, but read it carefully. It measures the change in outstanding positions, not money. Comparing monetary exposure across symbols means accounting for contract sizes and prices, which is why the value columns on the page are more useful than the contract count for that purpose.


### Volume is your reality check


An OI change with almost no volume behind it deserves suspicion. Thin trading can produce readings that do not reflect any real shift in positioning.


When both[volume](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-read-volume-in-an-option-chain) and open interest move together, you at least know real participation is behind the change.


## Using OI Spurts to Screen Stock F&O


Most retail attention sits on Nifty and Bank Nifty. This list covers the whole[F&O universe,](https://algotest.in/blog/futures-options-algo-trading-india) which means it surfaces names you would not otherwise have looked at.


A workable screening routine:


-


Sort by percentage change in open interest and take the top 15 to 20 names.


-


Drop anything where volume looks thin relative to the OI change.


-


Note whether the open interest rose or fell, because a build-up and an unwind point in opposite directions.


-


Pull up the price move for each remaining name, since open interest on its own tells you nothing about direction.


-


Switch to the contract view for anything interesting, to see which expiry and strike the activity sits in.


-


Check whether news explains the move, such as results, a corporate announcement or a sector event.


That last step matters. A stock with a large OI jump the day before its earnings could be hedging, speculation, or both at once. The data shows that positions were created. It cannot tell you why.

## What OI Spurts Cannot Tell You


-


An OI rise does not show direction on its own, because buyers and sellers both create positions. You need the price move alongside it.


-


It does not reveal motive, since a hedge and a directional bet produce the same OI increase.


-


It does not adjust for expiry. In the last few sessions before expiry, rollovers inflate OI in the next series and shrink it in the current one.


-


It does not show who is positioned. For that, use NSE’s participant-wise open interest report, which splits positions across FII, DII, Client and Pro. Our[participant-wise open interest](https://algotest.in/blog/participant-wise-open-interest/) guide explains how to read it.


## Common Mistakes When Reading OI Spurts


-


Many traders treat a high percentage change as a buy signal, even though the figure has no direction on its own.


-


Some read the By Underlying view and assume they know which strike the activity is in, when that needs the contract view.


-


Comparing absolute contract changes across symbols as if they were equal amounts of money gives a false picture.


-


Watching only OI increases means missing cases where a crowded position is being abandoned.


-


Checking the page once in the morning misses how much intraday OI can shift by the afternoon.


-


Screening the list and trading within the hour skips the step of testing whether the pattern has worked before.
